## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

The American Kennel Club (AKC) recently released its annual list of the most popular dog breeds, and this year’s results are largely similar to the last.
The French Bulldog maintained the title of the most popular dog breed in the U.S. for the fourth year in a row. But there were some shifts. The Dachshund moved up in popularity, securing a spot in the top five dog breeds for the first time, and the Bulldog swapped places with the German Shorthaired Pointer.
What other dog breeds were deemed the most popular in the country? We’ve got a rundown of the results, and what you can expect from each if you’re looking to add one of these sought-after breeds to your home.

### Key Takeaways
*   The French Bulldog has been the most popular dog breed since 2022.  
*   Before the Frenchie, the Labrador Retriever held the title of most popular dog for 31 years.  
*   Dachshunds and German Shorthaired Pointers both rose in popularity in 2025.   
*   Many popular dogs make great family dogs thanks to their friendly temperaments.

## 1. French Bulldog
Photo by Adobe Stock/otsphoto
TheFrench Bulldoghas been climbing the ranks in popularity over the last 10 years, according to the AKC. They were first named the most popular dog breed in 2022 and still hold that title today.
It’s not hard to see why—Frenchies, as they’re often called, are easygoing, happy, compact dogs with a good-natured temperament and a bright personality.
They enjoyshort walks, playing fetch, and games of tug-of-war. Their smaller size is ideal for any type of home, which has no doubt contributed to their popularity.
French Bulldogs are prone to a handful of health issues, though, includingbrachycephalic airway syndrome,ear infections, and back injuries.
Frenchies, like other breeds, should be fed a size and age-appropriate diet, and cleaning their ears regularly can help prevent frequent ear infections.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.
